Consider a classical many‑particle system with Hamiltonian  
\[ H(p,q)=\frac12 p^{\mathsf T}M^{-1}p+V(q),\qquad q\in\mathbb R^{d},\;p\in\mathbb R^{d}, \n\] where M is a positive‑definite mass matrix and the potential V(q) possesses two deep, well‑separated minima A and B separated by a first‑order saddle point at q^{\ddagger}.  
Let \Sigma be a smooth (d-1)-dimensional dividing surface defined implicitly by a scalar function \xi(q)=0 with \nabla\xi(q^{\ddagger})\neq0. The reactive flux through \Sigma at temperature T is  
\[ \Phi_{\Sigma}= \Big\langle \delta\bigl(\xi(q)\bigr)\,\bigl[\dot\xi(q,p)\bigr]_{+}\Big\rangle_{\!eq}, \n\] where [\dot\xi]_{+}=\max\{\dot\xi,0\} and \langle\cdot\rangle_{\!eq} denotes the canonical ensemble average. The conventional transition‑state theory (TST) rate constant is k_{\mathrm{TST}}=\Phi_{\Sigma}/\langle h_{A}\rangle_{\!eq}, with h_{A} the indicator of basin A.  
Define the transmission coefficient \kappa[\Sigma] as the ratio of the exact reactive rate k_{\mathrm{exact}} (obtained from the long‑time limit of the reactive flux correlation function) to the TST rate:  
\[ \kappa[\Sigma]=\frac{k_{\mathrm{exact}}}{k_{\mathrm{TST}}}. \] 
Suppose \kappa[\Sigma] is estimated by a Monte‑Carlo procedure that samples N independent phase‑space points on \Sigma and computes the empirical average  
\[ \hat\kappa = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} h_{B}\!\bigl(\Phi_{t_{i}}(q_{i},p_{i})\bigr), \n\] where each trajectory is propagated for a fixed “commitment time’’ t_{i}=t_{\mathrm{c}} long enough that h_{B} is effectively binary.  
Task 2 (Error Estimate for Numerical Evaluation) (a) Assuming the underlying Bernoulli variance \sigma^{2}= \kappa(1-\kappa), derive the standard error SE(\hat\kappa) and show that the relative error behaves as  
\[ \frac{\mathrm{SE}(\hat\kappa)}{\kappa}\;\sim\;\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\;\frac{1}{\sqrt{\kappa}}\qquad(\kappa\ll1). \]
unverified_model_answer:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Since }X_i=h_{B}(\Phi_{t_c}(q_i,p_i))\in\{0,1\},\qquad 
\mathbb{E}[X_i]=\kappa ,\;\; \operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\sigma^2=\kappa(1-\kappa).
\end{aligned}
\]

For \(N\) independent samples the estimator  

\[
\hat\kappa=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N X_i
\]

has variance  

\[
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\kappa)=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X_i)}{N}
   =\frac{\kappa(1-\kappa)}{N}.
\]

Hence the **standard error** is  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\mathrm{SE}(\hat\kappa)=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(\hat\kappa)}
   =\sqrt{\frac{\kappa(1-\kappa)}{N}} } .
\]

The relative error is  

\[
\frac{\mathrm{SE}(\hat\kappa)}{\kappa}
   =\sqrt{\frac{1-\kappa}{N\kappa}} .
\]

When the transmission coefficient is small (\(\kappa\ll1\)), \(1-\kappa\simeq1\) and  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\frac{\mathrm{SE}(\hat\kappa)}{\kappa}\;\sim\;
\frac{1}{\sqrt{N\kappa}}
   =\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\;\frac{1}{\sqrt{\kappa}}\qquad(\kappa\ll1).}
\]

Thus the relative statistical error grows as \(1/\sqrt{\kappa}\) for rare‑event (small \(\kappa\)) calculations.

Define the transmission coefficient \kappa[\Sigma] as the ratio of the exact reactive rate k_{\mathrm{exact}} (obtained from the long‑time limit of the reactive flux correlation function) to the TST rate:  
\[ \kappa[\Sigma]=\frac{k_{\mathrm{exact}}}{k_{\mathrm{TST}}}. \] 
Consider the two‑dimensional potential  
\[ V(x,y)=\frac{a}{4}\bigl(x^{2}-b^{2}\bigr)^{2}+ \frac{c}{2}y^{2}, \n\] with a,b,c>0. The minima are at (\pm b,0) and the saddle at the origin.  
The committor function q^{+}(q) is the probability that a trajectory initiated at q reaches basin B before basin A.  
Task 3 (Application to a Model Potential) (a) Compute the committor function q^{+}(x,y) analytically in the harmonic approximation near the saddle (i.e., linearize the dynamics and treat the unstable direction as x and the stable direction as y).

In the harmonic (quadratic) approximation the potential near the saddle \((0,0)\) is  

\[
V(x,y)\simeq V(0,0)+\frac12\Big[-\,a b^{2}\,x^{2}+c\,y^{2}\Big],
\qquad 
V(0,0)=\frac{a b^{4}}{4}.
\]

Hence the unstable direction is the \(x\)–coordinate (negative curvature) and the stable one is the \(y\)–coordinate (positive curvature).  
For overdamped Langevin dynamics at temperature \(T\) the backward Kolmogorov equation for the committor \(q^{+}(x,y)\) reads  

\[
D\,\partial_{x}^{2}q^{+}+ \frac{a b^{2}}{\gamma}\,x\,\partial_{x}q^{+}
      + D\,\partial_{y}^{2}q^{+}-\frac{c}{\gamma}\,y\,\partial_{y}q^{+}=0,
\qquad D=\frac{k_{B}T}{\gamma}.
\]

Because the stable \(y\)‑direction is confined, the solution is independent of \(y\) and satisfies the one‑dimensional ODE  

\[
D\,\frac{d^{2}q}{dx^{2}}+\frac{a b^{2}}{\gamma}\,x\,\frac{dq}{dx}=0,
\qquad q(-\infty)=0,\; q(+\infty)=1 .
\]

Writing \(\lambda = a b^{2}/\gamma\) and solving,
\[
\frac{dq}{dx}=C\exp\!\Big[-\frac{\lambda}{2D}x^{2}\Big],
\qquad 
q(x)=C\int_{-\infty}^{x}\exp\!\Big[-\frac{\lambda}{2D}s^{2}\Big]ds .
\]

\[

Consider a side‑chain liquid‑crystal elastomer (LCE) in its nematic phase. The material can be prepared either as a **mono‑domain** sample, in which the nematic director **n̂** is uniform throughout the sample, or as a **polydomain** sample, in which the director orientation varies randomly from domain to domain. The polymer backbone dynamics are well described by the **Rouse model**, while the nematic director relaxes with a characteristic Debye‑type relaxation time **τₙ**.

When a simple shear deformation of amplitude γ₀ sin ωt is applied, the measured complex shear modulus

\[ G^{*}(\omega)=G'(\omega)+iG''(\omega) \]

depends on whether the shear direction is **parallel** (‖) or **perpendicular** (⊥) to the uniform director in the mono‑domain case. The total stress is assumed to be the linear superposition of a polymeric contribution and a nematic contribution that couples to the shear through a scalar coupling constant **λ**.

The polymeric (Rouse) contribution to the storage modulus can be approximated by

\[ G_{\text{R}}(\omega)=
\begin{cases}
G_{0}\,\omega\tau_{\text{R}}, & \omega\tau_{\text{R}}\ll 1,\\[4pt]
G_{0}\,(\omega\tau_{\text{R}})^{1/2}, & \omega\tau_{\text{R}}\gg 1,
\end{cases}
\]

where **G₀** is a characteristic modulus and **τ_R** the Rouse relaxation time.

The nematic contribution is modeled as a Debye relaxation

\[ G_{\text{n}}(\omega)=\frac{\Delta G}{1+i\omega\tau_{n}}, \]

with **ΔG** the strength of the nematic elastic response.

**(a) Derivation of the anisotropic storage modulus**

Write the total storage modulus for shear **parallel** and **perpendicular** to the director as

\[ G'_{\parallel}(\omega)=G_{\text{R}}'(\omega)+\lambda\,G_{\text{n}}'(\omega),\qquad
G'_{\perp}(\omega)=G_{\text{R}}'(\omega)-\lambda\,G_{\text{n}}'(\omega), \]

where the prime denotes the real part of the complex modulus.

1. Express \(G_{\text{n}}'(\omega)\) explicitly in terms of \(\Delta G\), \(\omega\), and \(\tau_{n}\).
2. Combine the expressions to obtain the **anisotropy**

\[ \Delta G'(\omega)=G'_{\parallel}(\omega)-G'_{\perp}(\omega) \]

as a closed‑form function of \(\omega\), \(\lambda\), \(\Delta G\), \(\tau_{n}\), and the appropriate asymptotic form of \(G_{\text{R}}'(\omega)\).
unverified_model_answer:
The nematic Debye term gives  

\[
G_{\text n}(\omega)=\frac{\Delta G}{1+i\omega\tau_n}
      =\frac{\Delta G\,(1-i\omega\tau_n)}{1+(\omega\tau_n)^2}\,,
\]

so its real (storage) part is  

\[
\boxed{\,G_{\text n}'(\omega)=\frac{\Delta G}{1+(\omega\tau_n)^2}\,}.
\]

Hence  

\[
\begin{aligned}
G'_{\parallel}(\omega)&=G_{\text R}'(\omega)+\lambda\,\frac{\Delta G}{1+(\omega\tau_n)^2},\\[4pt]
G'_{\perp}(\omega)&=G_{\text R}'(\omega)-\lambda\,\frac{\Delta G}{1+(\omega\tau_n)^2},
\end{aligned}
\]

with the polymeric storage modulus  

\[
G_{\text R}'(\omega)\simeq 
\begin{cases}
G_{0}\,\omega\tau_{\text R}, & \omega\tau_{\text R}\ll1,\\[4pt]
G_{0}\,(\omega\tau_{\text R})^{1/2}, & \omega\tau_{\text R}\gg1 .
\end{cases}
\]

Subtracting the two directions eliminates the polymeric term, giving the anisotropy

\[
\boxed{\Delta G'(\omega)=G'_{\parallel}(\omega)-G'_{\perp}(\omega)
      =\frac{2\,\lambda\,\Delta G}{1+(\omega\tau_n)^2}} .
\]

  1. CO₂ + e⁻ ⇌ CO₂·⁻_ads                        (fast quasi‑equilibrium)
  2. CO₂·⁻_ads + H⁺ + e⁻ → *CO + H₂O             (rate‑determining step, RDS)

* **Pathway B (concerted proton‑coupled electron transfer, PCET)**
  CO₂ + H₂O + 2 e⁻ → *CO + 2 OH⁻                     (single RDS)

Assume that (i) the surface coverage of *CO is low, (ii) CO₂ mass transport is not limiting, and (iii) the activity of water is unity. In the potential window –0.20 V ≤ η ≤ –0.40 V vs SHE the measured current density obeys a Tafel relationship

i = i_0 \exp\!\left(\frac{\alpha F \eta}{RT}\right)

with an apparent Tafel slope of **120 mV dec⁻¹**. Simultaneously, the reaction order with respect to bulk CO₂ concentration, \(c_{\mathrm{CO_2}}\), is experimentally found to be **0.5** in the same potential range.

### (a) Derive the theoretical Tafel slope and CO₂ reaction order for each pathway.

1. **Pathway A**
   - Write the rate expression for the RDS (step 2) using transition‑state theory:

     r_A = k_A\,\theta_{\mathrm{CO_2·^-}}\,a_{\mathrm{H^+}}\,\exp\!\left(-\frac{\beta_A F \eta}{RT}\right)

     where \(k_A\) incorporates the standard rate constant, \(\beta_A\) is the symmetry factor for the electron transfer in step 2, and \(\theta_{\mathrm{CO_2·^-}}\) is the surface coverage of the adsorbed radical anion.
   - From the fast equilibrium of step 1,

     K_1 = \frac{\theta_{\mathrm{CO_2·^-}}}{c_{\mathrm{CO_2}}\,\exp\!\left(-\frac{\alpha_1 F \eta}{RT}\right)}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\theta_{\mathrm{CO_2·^-}} = K_1\,c_{\mathrm{CO_2}}\,\exp\!\left(\frac{\alpha_1 F \eta}{RT}\right)

   - Substituting into \(r_A\) and noting that the measured current \(i = nF r_A\) (with \(n=2\) electrons per CO formed) gives

     i_A = i_{0A}\;c_{\mathrm{CO_2}}\;\exp\!\left[\frac{(\alpha_1-\beta_A)F\eta}{RT}\right]

   - Hence the **apparent Tafel slope** for pathway A is

     b_A = \frac{2.303\,RT}{(\beta_A-\alpha_1)F}

     and the **reaction order** with respect to CO₂ is

     \rho_A = 1 \quad\text{(first order in }c_{\mathrm{CO_2}}\text{)}.

2. **Pathway B**
   - For the concerted PCET step, the rate expression is

     r_B = k_B\,c_{\mathrm{CO_2}}\,\exp\!\left(-\frac{\beta_B F \eta}{RT}\right)

     because water activity is unity and the electron‑proton transfer occurs in a single elementary step.
   - The current density becomes

     i_B = i_{0B}\;c_{\mathrm{CO_2}}^{\,\gamma}\;\exp\!\left(\frac{\alpha_B F\eta}{RT}\right)

     where \(\gamma\) is the kinetic order in CO₂ that emerges from the transition‑state dependence on CO₂ concentration. For a truly bimolecular elementary step involving CO₂ and H₂O, transition‑state theory predicts a **half‑order** dependence on CO₂ (the square‑root term appears when the transition state involves a pre‑association equilibrium). Thus we set \(\gamma = 1/2\).

   - Consequently, the **Tafel slope** for pathway B is

     b_B = \frac{2.303\,RT}{\alpha_B F}

     and the **reaction order** is

     \rho_B = \frac{1}{2}.

| Pathway | Tafel slope \(b\) (V dec⁻¹) | Reaction order \(\rho\) |
|---------|----------------------------|--------------------------|
| A       | \(b_A = \dfrac{2.303RT}{(\beta_A-\alpha_1)F}\) | 1 |
| B       | \(b_B = \dfrac{2.303RT}{\alpha_B F}\)          | ½ |

A family of low‑molecular‑weight gelators (LMWGs) consists of bis‑urea molecules that self‑assemble through urea–urea hydrogen bonding into extended two‑dimensional sheets (α‑tape motifs). Each sheet possesses two chemically distinct faces, *F₁* and *F₂*, because of an asymmetric spacer attached to the urea groups. The surface free energies of the two faces are γ₁ and γ₂ (γ₁ > γ₂).

When a nascent sheet is formed in solution it can follow one of two competing pathways:

1. **Planar crystal growth** – the sheet extends laterally, adding rows of molecules without bending.
2. **Scroll formation** – the sheet bends and rolls up into a cylindrical scroll (radius *R*), exposing the lower‑energy face *F₂* on the outer surface and the higher‑energy face *F₁* on the inner surface.

Assume the following thermodynamic and kinetic model:

* The bending energy per unit length of a scroll of radius *R* is given by  
  \[
  E_{\text{bend}}(R)=\frac{\kappa}{2R^{2}}\, ,
  \]
  where κ is the bending modulus of the sheet (units J·m).

* The interfacial free‑energy contribution per unit length associated with the asymmetry of the two faces is  
  \[
  E_{\text{asym}}(R)=2\pi R(\gamma_{1}-\gamma_{2})\, ,
  \]
  because the inner surface of the scroll (area = 2πR × 1 m) is coated by *F₁* and the outer surface by *F₂*.

* The total free‑energy change per unit length upon scrolling from a flat sheet (reference state) is therefore  
  \[
  \Delta G(R)=E_{\text{bend}}(R)+E_{\text{asym}}(R)-\Delta\mu\, ,
  \]
  where Δμ (>0) is the bulk free‑energy gain per unit length from adding molecules to the crystal (i.e., the driving force for planar growth).

* The kinetic competition between the two pathways is described by Arrhenius‑type rates:  
  \[
  k_{\text{scroll}}=A_{\text{s}}\exp\!\left[-\frac{E_{\text{act,s}}}{k_{\text{B}}T}\right],\qquad
  k_{\text{cryst}}=A_{\text{c}}\exp\!\left[-\frac{E_{\text{act,c}}}{k_{\text{B}}T}\right],
  \]
  where the activation barriers are approximated by the corresponding free‑energy changes:  
  \[
  E_{\text{act,s}}\approx \Delta G(R^{*}),\qquad 
  E_{\text{act,c}}\approx -\Delta\mu .
  \]
  *R*⁎ is the radius that minimizes ΔG(R).

* Photoisomerisation of a terminal imine group can only occur when the imine is free to rotate, which is possible only if the molecule resides on the outer surface of a scroll (face *F₂*). If the molecule is incorporated into a planar crystal or is buried on the inner surface of a scroll, rotation is sterically blocked.

---

**(a) Derive the optimal scroll radius *R*⁎ that minimizes ΔG(R). Show that it satisfies a simple algebraic relation and give the explicit expression for *R*⁎ in terms of κ, γ₁ − γ₂, and Δμ.**
unverified_model_answer:
The total free‑energy change per unit length for a scroll of radius \(R\) is  

\[
\Delta G(R)=\frac{\kappa}{2R^{2}}+2\pi R(\gamma_{1}-\gamma_{2})-\Delta\mu .
\]

The optimum radius \(R^{*}\) follows from  

\[
\frac{d\Delta G}{dR}=0\;.
\]

Since \(\Delta\mu\) is a constant,  

\[
\frac{d\Delta G}{dR}= -\frac{\kappa}{R^{3}}+2\pi(\gamma_{1}-\gamma_{2})=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{\kappa}{R^{3}}=2\pi(\gamma_{1}-\gamma_{2}).
\]

Hence the optimal radius satisfies the simple algebraic relation  

\[
\boxed{\;\kappa = 2\pi(\gamma_{1}-\gamma_{2})\,R^{*\,3}\;}
\]

and solving for \(R^{*}\) gives  

\[
\boxed{R^{*}= \left[\frac{\kappa}{2\pi(\gamma_{1}-\gamma_{2})}\right]^{\!1/3}}.
\]

(The bulk driving force \(\Delta\mu\) does not affect the location of the minimum; it only determines whether \(\Delta G(R^{*})\) is negative, i.e. whether scrolling is thermodynamically favorable.)

Consider a series of β‑substituted ethyl radicals of the form R–CH₂–CH₂·, where the β‑carbon bears a substituent Y (Y = PH₂, SH, or Cl).

1. Hyperconjugative Stabilization Energy
   Using second‑order perturbation theory as implemented in Natural Bond Orbital (NBO) analysis, derive the expression for the hyperconjugative stabilization energy Eₕc arising from the interaction between the singly‑occupied molecular orbital (SOMO) localized on the α‑carbon radical center and the σ(Cβ–Y) bonding orbital. Clearly define all terms (e.g., Fock matrix elements, energy denominators) and indicate any assumptions made about orbital orthogonality and occupancy.
unverified_model_answer:
The hyperconjugative interaction is treated as a donor → acceptor second‑order perturbation in the NBO framework.  
For a filled donor NBO \(i\) (occupancy \(n_i\)) interacting with an empty or partially‑filled acceptor NBO \(j\) the second‑order energy correction is  

\[
E^{(2)}_{ij}= -\,\frac{n_i\;(F_{ij})^{2}}{\varepsilon_j-\varepsilon_i}\;,
\]

where  

* \(F_{ij}= \langle i|\,\hat F\,|j\rangle\) is the off‑diagonal Fock matrix element between the two NBOs,  
* \(\varepsilon_i=\langle i|\,\hat F\,|i\rangle\) and \(\varepsilon_j=\langle j|\,\hat F\,|j\rangle\) are the diagonal Fock (orbital‑energy) elements,  
* \(n_i\) is the occupancy of the donor NBO (2 e⁻ for a σ bond),  
* the denominator \(\Delta\varepsilon=\varepsilon_j-\varepsilon_i\) is the energy gap between acceptor and donor (positive for a higher‑energy acceptor).  

In the β‑substituted ethyl radicals the donor is the σ(Cβ–Y) bonding orbital (i = σ) and the acceptor is the α‑carbon SOMO (j = SOMO).  Assuming the NBOs are orthogonal and that the interaction is weak enough for second‑order perturbation theory to be valid, the hyperconjugative stabilization energy becomes  

\[
E_{\mathrm{hc}} = -\,\frac{n_{\sigma}\;(F_{\sigma,\mathrm{SOMO}})^{2}}{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{SOMO}}-\varepsilon_{\sigma}}
               = -\,\frac{2\;(F_{\sigma\!\to\!\mathrm{SOMO}})^{2}}{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{SOMO}}-\varepsilon_{\sigma}} .
\]

Because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{SOMO}} > \varepsilon_{\sigma}\), the denominator \(\Delta\varepsilon\) is positive, so the interaction lowers the total energy (stabilization).  The magnitude of the stabilization is often reported as a positive quantity:

\[
|E_{\mathrm{hc}}| = \frac{2\;(F_{\sigma\!\to\!\mathrm{SOMO}})^{2}}{\Delta\varepsilon}.
\]

\[
\boxed{E_{\mathrm{hc}} = -\,\dfrac{2\;\bigl(F_{\sigma\!\to\!\mathrm{SOMO}}\bigr)^{2}}{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{SOMO}} - \varepsilon_{\sigma}} \;=\; \dfrac{2\;(F_{\sigma\!\to\!\mathrm{SOMO}})^{2}}{\Delta\varepsilon}}
\]

Consider a vertically oriented, cylindrical fluidized bed of height H and diameter D containing uniform spherical particles of diameter d_p, density rho_p, and porosity epsilon. The bed is operated at an absolute pressure P and temperature T, with a gas of molecular weight M and constant specific heat ratio gamma introduced from the bottom at a superficial (cross‑sectional) velocity U_0.

The gas density and dynamic viscosity at the operating conditions are given by the ideal‑gas relations:

rho_g = P M / (R T),   mu_g = mu_0 (T/T_0)^n,

where mu_0, T_0 and n are known reference values.

Inside the bed, gas flows through a network of bubbles that rise vertically. For a single bubble of radius R_b(z) at height z, the gas velocity inside the bubble, U_b(z), is related to the superficial velocity by a void‑fraction balance:

U_0 = epsilon(z) * U_s(z) + alpha(z) * U_b(z),

where U_s(z) is the interstitial gas velocity in the emulsion (particle‑filled) phase, and alpha(z) is the local bubble volume fraction (void fraction contributed by bubbles).

The drag force per unit volume exerted by the gas on the particles in the emulsion phase can be expressed by the Ergun equation:

f_D(z) = 150 (1 - epsilon(z))^2 mu_g U_s(z) / (d_p^2 epsilon(z)^3) + 1.75 (1 - epsilon(z)) rho_g U_s(z)^2 / (d_p epsilon(z)^3).

Stability analysis of the drag force under velocity fluctuations (a): Let the interstitial gas velocity contain a small fluctuating component, U_s(z,t) = U_s_bar(z) + u'(z,t) with |u'| << U_s_bar. Linearize the Ergun drag expression about the mean state to obtain the first‑order perturbation in drag, delta_f_D(z,t). Show that

delta_f_D(z,t) ≈ [ 150 (1-ε)^2 μ_g / (d_p^2 ε^3) + 3.5 (1-ε) ρ_g U_s_bar / (d_p ε^3) ] u'(z,t).

The Ergun drag per unit volume can be written as  

\[
f_D(U_s)=A\,U_s+B\,U_s^{2},
\qquad 
A=\frac{150(1-\varepsilon)^{2}\mu_g}{d_p^{2}\varepsilon^{3}},\;
B=\frac{1.75(1-\varepsilon)\rho_g}{d_p\varepsilon^{3}} .
\]

Introduce a small perturbation \(U_s(z,t)=\overline{U}_s(z)+u'(z,t)\) with \(|u'|\ll\overline{U}_s\).  
A Taylor expansion about the mean state gives  

\[
\begin{aligned}
f_D(U_s) &\approx A(\overline{U}_s+u')+B(\overline{U}_s+u')^{2}\\
&=A\overline{U}_s+B\overline{U}_s^{2}+\bigl(A+2B\overline{U}_s\bigr)u'+\mathcal{O}(u'^{2}) .
\end{aligned}
\]

The first term is the mean drag \(\overline{f}_D\); the linear perturbation is  

\[
\delta f_D(z,t)=\bigl(A+2B\overline{U}_s\bigr)u'(z,t).
\]

Substituting \(A\) and \(B\) yields  

\[
\delta f_D(z,t)=\left[\,\frac{150(1-\varepsilon)^{2}\mu_g}{d_p^{2}\varepsilon^{3}}
+\frac{3.5(1-\varepsilon)\rho_g\overline{U}_s}{d_p\varepsilon^{3}}\,\right]u'(z,t).
\]

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\delta f_D(z,t)\;\approx\;
\Bigg[\,\frac{150 (1-\varepsilon)^{2}\,\mu_g}{d_p^{2}\,\varepsilon^{3}}
\;+\;\frac{3.5 (1-\varepsilon)\,\rho_g\,\overline{U}_s}{d_p\,\varepsilon^{3}}\,\Bigg]\,
u'(z,t)}
\]

The excess Gibbs energy of a liquid mixture is defined as  

\[
G^{E}=RT\sum_{i=1}^{3}n_i\ln\gamma_i
      =RT\,n\sum_{i=1}^{3}x_i\ln\gamma_i,
\qquad 
x_i=\frac{n_i}{n},\;\; \sum_i x_i=1 .
\]

Dividing by the total number of moles \(n\) gives the molar excess Gibbs energy  

\[
g^{E}\equiv\frac{G^{E}}{n}=RT\sum_{i=1}^{3}x_i\ln\gamma_i .
\tag{1}
\]

### Differential of \(g^{E}\)

At constant temperature and pressure  

\[
\mathrm d g^{E}=RT\sum_{i=1}^{3}\Bigl(\ln\gamma_i\,\mathrm d x_i
                     +x_i\,\mathrm d\ln\gamma_i\Bigr).
\tag{2}
\]

Because the mole fractions always satisfy \(\sum_i x_i=1\),

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{3}\mathrm d x_i =0 .
\tag{3}
\]

Hence the term containing \(\ln\gamma_i\) vanishes when the total differential of the excess Gibbs energy is expressed in terms of composition changes:

\[
\mathrm d g^{E}=RT\sum_{i=1}^{3}x_i\,\mathrm d\ln\gamma_i .
\tag{4}
\]

---

### Gibbs–Duhem relation

The excess Gibbs energy is a **homogeneous first‑order** function of the mole numbers.  By Euler’s theorem  

\[
G^{E}= \sum_{i=1}^{3} n_i\mu_i^{E},
\qquad\text{with}\quad \mu_i^{E}=RT\ln\gamma_i .
\]

Differentiating and using the Gibbs–Duhem theorem for the excess part,  

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{3} n_i\,\mathrm d\mu_i^{E}=0
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
\sum_{i=1}^{3} x_i\,\mathrm d\mu_i^{E}=0 .
\]

Substituting \(\mu_i^{E}=RT\ln\gamma_i\) gives the **Gibbs–Duhem relation for the activity coefficients**:

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{3} x_i\,\mathrm d\ln\gamma_i = 0 } .
\]

\[
g^{E}=RT\sum_{i=1}^{3}x_i\ln\gamma_i,
\qquad 
\text{and}\qquad 
\sum_{i=1}^{3}x_i\,\mathrm d\ln\gamma_i=0 .
\]

| Quantity | Value |
|----------|-------|
| Electric dipole moment of A, \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_A\) | \(2.0\;\text{D}\) |
| Electric dipole moment of B, \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_B\) | \(1.5\;\text{D}\) |
| Magnetic dipole moment of A, \(\boldsymbol{m}_A\) | \(0.10\;\mu_{\mathrm{B}}\) |
| Magnetic dipole moment of B, \(\boldsymbol{m}_B\) | \(0.08\;\mu_{\mathrm{B}}\) |
| Scalar product \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_A\!\cdot\!\boldsymbol{\mu}_B\) | \(2.5\;\text{D}^2\) |
| Scalar product \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_A\!\cdot\!\boldsymbol{m}_B\) | \(0.15\;\text{D}\,\mu_{\mathrm{B}}\) |
| Scalar product \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_B\!\cdot\!\boldsymbol{m}_A\) | \(0.12\;\text{D}\,\mu_{\mathrm{B}}\) |
| Dipole–dipole coupling constant, \(\kappa\) | \(0.05\;\text{Å}^{-3}\) |

The Rosenfeld equation relates the rotatory strength \(R_k\) of transition \(k\) to the electric and magnetic transition dipole moments:

\[R_k = \operatorname{Im}\!\big(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k \cdot \boldsymbol{m}_k\big).\]

In a dipole–dipole coupling approximation, the interaction contribution to the rotatory strength can be written as a bilinear function of the transition moments of the two centers, scaled by \(\kappa\).

The specific rotation \([α]\) (in the conventional units) is related to the sum of rotatory strengths by

\[[α] = \frac{72.0\times10^{6}}{c\,M\,\lambda^{2}} \sum_k R_k,\]

where \(c = 2.998\times10^{10}\;\text{cm·s}^{-1}\) is the speed of light, \(M\) is the molar mass of the molecule (take \(M = 300\;\text{g·mol}^{-1}\)), and \(\lambda\) is the wavelength expressed in centimeters.

**(a)** Derive an explicit expression for the interaction term \(\Delta α_{\text{int}}\) in terms of the given dipole moments, scalar products, and the coupling constant \(\kappa\), starting from the Rosenfeld equation and employing a dipole–dipole coupling model. Clearly state any approximations you make.

**Derivation**

1. **Total rotatory strength of the dimer**  

   For a molecule that contains two chromophoric stereogenic centres A and B the total rotatory strength of a given electronic transition \(k\) can be written as the sum of the individual (intrinsic) contributions and an interaction term that originates from the coupling of the two centres:

   \[
   R_k^{\text{(dimer)}} = R_k^{(A)}+R_k^{(B)}+R_k^{\text{int}} .
   \]

   The Rosenfeld equation gives the intrinsic rotatory strengths

   \[
   R_k^{(A)} = \operatorname{Im}\!\big(\boldsymbol{\mu}_A\!\cdot\!\boldsymbol{m}_A\big),\qquad 
   R_k^{(B)} = \operatorname{Im}\!\big(\boldsymbol{\mu}_B\!\cdot\!\boldsymbol{m}_B\big) .
   \]

2. **Dipole–dipole coupling model**  

   In the dipole–dipole approximation the electric dipole of one centre perturbs the magnetic dipole of the other.  To first order the effective magnetic transition dipole moments become

   \[
   \boldsymbol{m}_A^{\text{eff}} \simeq \boldsymbol{m}_A + \kappa\,\boldsymbol{\mu}_B ,\qquad
   \boldsymbol{m}_B^{\text{eff}} \simeq \boldsymbol{m}_B + \kappa\,\boldsymbol{\mu}_A ,
   \]

   where \(\kappa\) (units Å\(^{-3}\)) is the dipole–dipole coupling constant that contains the geometric factor \(1/R^{3}\) (with \(R\) the centre‑centre distance) and the orientational averaging.

3. **Interaction contribution to the rotatory strength**  

   Substituting the effective magnetic dipoles into the Rosenfeld expression and retaining only the cross‑terms that are linear in \(\kappa\) gives

   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   R_k^{\text{int}} &=
   \operatorname{Im}\!\big[\,\boldsymbol{\mu}_A\!\cdot\!(\kappa\boldsymbol{\mu}_B)
   +\boldsymbol{\mu}_B\!\cdot\!(\kappa\boldsymbol{\mu}_A)\,\big] \\
   &\quad +\operatorname{Im}\!\big[\,\boldsymbol{\mu}_A\!\cdot\!\boldsymbol{m}_B
   +\boldsymbol{\mu}_B\!\cdot\!\boldsymbol{m}_A\,\big]\kappa .
   \end{aligned}
   \]

   The scalar products \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_A\!\cdot\!\boldsymbol{\mu}_B\) are real, therefore their imaginary parts vanish.  The only surviving term is the bilinear electric–magnetic product, which yields

   \[
   R_k^{\text{int}} \;\approx\; \kappa\Big[\,\boldsymbol{\mu}_A\!\cdot\!\boldsymbol{m}_B
   +\boldsymbol{\mu}_B\!\cdot\!\boldsymbol{m}_A\,\Big] .
   \]

   This is the desired bilinear form, expressed entirely in terms of the given scalar products.

4. **From rotatory strength to specific rotation**  

   The specific rotation for a transition centred at wavelength \(\lambda\) is related to the rotatory strength by the Rosenfeld‑derived formula

   \[
   [\alpha] = \frac{72.0\times10^{6}}{c\,M\,\lambda^{2}}\,R_k .
   \]

   Consequently, the interaction contribution to the observed specific rotation of the dimer is

   \[
   \Delta\alpha_{\text{int}} = 
   \frac{72.0\times10^{6}}{c\,M\,\lambda^{2}}\,R_k^{\text{int}} .
   \]

5. **Explicit expression for \(\Delta\alpha_{\text{int}}\)**  

   Inserting the expression for \(R_k^{\text{int}}\) obtained in step 3 gives

   \[
   \boxed{\;
   \Delta\alpha_{\text{int}} \;=\;
   \frac{72.0\times10^{6}\,\kappa}{c\,M\,\lambda^{2}}\,
   \Big[\,(\boldsymbol{\mu}_A\!\cdot\!\boldsymbol{m}_B)
   +(\boldsymbol{\mu}_B\!\cdot\!\boldsymbol{m}_A)\,\Big]
   \;}
   \]

   where the scalar products are the experimentally or theoretically determined values
   \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_A\!\cdot\!\boldsymbol{m}_B = 0.15\;{\rm D}\,\mu_{\mathrm B}\) and
   \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_B\!\cdot\!\boldsymbol{m}_A = 0.12\;{\rm D}\,\mu_{\mathrm B}\).

---

**Approximations made**

* Only the leading‑order dipole–dipole coupling (first order in \(\kappa\)) is retained; higher‑order multipole terms are neglected.  
* Transition dipole moments are treated as real vectors; any phase arising from the coupling is assumed to be encapsulated in the factor \(\kappa\) so that the cross‑products become effectively imaginary and contribute to the rotatory strength.  
* Rotational averaging of the relative orientation of the two centres is absorbed into the numerical value of \(\kappa\).  
* Solvent, temperature and vibrational contributions to the rotatory strength are ignored.

Consider a molecular dynamics study of the solidification of supercooled water into hexagonal ice (ice Iₕ). Growth proceeds by the attachment of water molecules to a crystalline interface, but before incorporation the molecules form transient two‑dimensional clusters (or "pre‐critical nuclei") within the interfacial layer. Two distinct cluster motifs are observed:

* **Hexagonal motif (H):** locally matches the ice Iₕ stacking (ABAB…) and is thermodynamically favorable.  
* **Cubic motif (C):** locally matches the cubic ice stacking (ABC…) and is metastable relative to H.

For a given crystallographic face *f* (either the basal {0001} face or a prism {10‑{10}/{11‑{20}} face) the following kinetic model is proposed:

1. A water molecule arriving at the interface first forms either an H‑ or C‑ motif with probabilities \(P_f^{\mathrm{H}}\) and \(P_f^{\mathrm{C}} = 1-P_f^{\mathrm{H}}\), respectively. These probabilities are face‑dependent because of differing local geometry and hydrogen‑bonding constraints.

2. Once formed, a motif persists for a stochastic lifetime \(\tau\) before either (i) rearranging into the stable ice lattice (successful attachment) or (ii) dissolving back into the liquid. The mean lifetimes are \(\langle \tau_f^{\mathrm{H}} \rangle\) and \(\langle \tau_f^{\mathrm{C}} \rangle\).  

3. The probability that a motif survives long enough to be incorporated into the crystal is given by an Arrhenius factor
\[\Phi_f^{\alpha}= \exp\!\left[-\frac{\Delta G_f^{\alpha}}{k_{\mathrm B}T}\right],\qquad \alpha\in\{\mathrm{H},\mathrm{C}\},\]
where \(\Delta G_f^{\alpha}\) is the free‑energy barrier for conversion of motif \(\alpha\) into the lattice on face *f*.

4. The net attachment flux \(J_f\) (molecules• area\(^{-1}\) • time\(^{-1}\)) on face *f* is therefore
\[J_f = \rho_{\ell}\,v_{\mathrm{th}} \Big[ P_f^{\mathrm{H}}\,\Phi_f^{\mathrm{H}} + P_f^{\mathrm{C}}\,\Phi_f^{\mathrm{C}} \Big],\]
where \(\rho_{\ell}\) is the liquid number density and \(v_{\mathrm{th}}=\sqrt{8k_{\mathrm B}T/(\pi m)}\) is the thermal velocity of water molecules (mass \(m\)).

5. The normal growth velocity of the face is \(v_f = \Omega\,J_f\), where \(\Omega\) is the molecular volume in the solid.

**(a)** Derive an explicit expression for the anisotropy ratio \(R = v_{\text{basal}}/v_{\text{prism}}\) in terms of the face‑dependent probabilities \(P_f^{\mathrm{H}}\), the free‑energy barriers \(\Delta G_f^{\alpha}\), and the temperature \(T\). Show how the lifetimes \(\langle \tau_f^{\alpha}\rangle\) can be incorporated into the barriers if one assumes \(\Delta G_f^{\alpha}=E_f^{\alpha} - k_{\mathrm B}T\ln\big(\langle \tau_f^{\alpha}\rangle/\tau_0\big)\), where \(E_f^{\alpha}\) is an intrinsic activation energy and \(\tau_0\) a microscopic attempt time.
unverified_model_answer:
The normal growth velocity of a crystal face *f* follows from the kinetic model as  

\[
v_f=\Omega J_f
   =\Omega \,\rho_{\ell}v_{\rm th}\Big[\,P_f^{\rm H}\,\Phi_f^{\rm H}
   +(1-P_f^{\rm H})\,\Phi_f^{\rm C}\Big],
\qquad 
\Phi_f^{\alpha}=e^{-\Delta G_f^{\alpha}/(k_{\!B}T)} .
\]

Because the liquid density \(\rho_{\ell}\), the thermal speed \(v_{\rm th}\) and the molecular volume \(\Omega\) are the same for the basal and prism faces, they cancel in the ratio of the two velocities.  Hence the anisotropy ratio  

\[
R\equiv\frac{v_{\rm basal}}{v_{\rm prism}}
      =\frac{J_{\rm basal}}{J_{\rm prism}}
\]

is

\[
\boxed{
R=
\frac{P_{\rm basal}^{\rm H}\,
      e^{-\Delta G_{\rm basal}^{\rm H}/(k_{\!B}T)}
      +(1-P_{\rm basal}^{\rm H})\,
      e^{-\Delta G_{\rm basal}^{\rm C}/(k_{\!B}T)}}
     {P_{\rm prism}^{\rm H}\,
      e^{-\Delta G_{\rm prism}^{\rm H}/(k_{\!B}T)}
      +(1-P_{\rm prism}^{\rm H})\,
      e^{-\Delta G_{\rm prism}^{\rm C}/(k_{\!B}T)}} } .
\]

---

### Incorporating the lifetimes of the motifs  

If the free‑energy barrier for conversion of a motif \(\alpha\) on face *f* is written as  

\[
\Delta G_f^{\alpha}=E_f^{\alpha}
                    -k_{\!B}T\ln\!\Big(\frac{\langle\tau_f^{\alpha}\rangle}{\tau_0}\Big),
\]

with an intrinsic activation energy \(E_f^{\alpha}\) and a microscopic attempt time \(\tau_0\), then  

\[
\Phi_f^{\alpha}
   =\exp\!\Big[-\frac{E_f^{\alpha}}{k_{\!B}T}\Big]\,
     \exp\!\Big[\ln\!\Big(\frac{\langle\tau_f^{\alpha}\rangle}{\tau_0}\Big)\Big]
   =\frac{\langle\tau_f^{\alpha}\rangle}{\tau_0}\,
     \exp\!\Big[-\frac{E_f^{\alpha}}{k_{\!B}T}\Big].
\]

Substituting this form of \(\Phi_f^{\alpha}\) into the expression for \(R\) gives

\[
\boxed{
R=
\frac{P_{\rm basal}^{\rm H}\,\langle\tau_{\rm basal}^{\rm H}\rangle\,
      e^{-E_{\rm basal}^{\rm H}/(k_{\!B}T)}
      +(1-P_{\rm basal}^{\rm H})\,\langle\tau_{\rm basal}^{\rm C}\rangle\,
      e^{-E_{\rm basal}^{\rm C}/(k_{\!B}T)}}
     {P_{\rm prism}^{\rm H}\,\langle\tau_{\rm prism}^{\rm H}\rangle\,
      e^{-E_{\rm prism}^{\rm H}/(k_{\!B}T)}
      +(1-P_{\rm prism}^{\rm H})\,\langle\tau_{\rm prism}^{\rm C}\rangle\,
      e^{-E_{\rm prism}^{\rm C}/(k_{\!B}T)}} } .
\]

(The factor \(1/\tau_0\) cancels from numerator and denominator.)  

Thus the anisotropy ratio is completely determined by the face‑dependent probabilities of forming the hexagonal motif, the intrinsic activation energies for conversion, the average lifetimes of the motifs, and the temperature.

3. A non‑retarded vdW attraction term,
   $$U_{\text{vdW}}(r) = -\frac{A_{ij}}{6}\left[\frac{2a_i a_j}{r^2-(a_i-a_j)^2} + \frac{2a_i a_j}{r^2-(a_i+a_j)^2} + \ln\frac{r^2-(a_i+a_j)^2}{r^2-(a_i-a_j)^2}\right],$$

\[ \phi(z)= rac{\sigma}{\varepsilon\kappa}\,e^{-\kappa z}, \qquad U_{	ext{el}}(z)=q\,\phi(z) = - rac{e\sigma}{\varepsilon\kappa}\,e^{-\kappa z}, \] 

where \( q=-e \) is the ion charge.  

2. **Partial desolvation penalty** as the ion approaches the interface, modeled by an exponential repulsive term  

\[ U_{	ext{des}}(z)=U_{0}\,e^{-(z-a)/\lambda}, \] 

with \( U_{0}>0 \) the desolvation energy at contact (\( z=a \)) and \( \lambda \) a characteristic decay length of the solvent structure (on the order of a molecular diameter).  

The total Gibbs free‑energy profile is therefore  

\[ G(z)=G_{\infty}+U_{	ext{el}}(z)+U_{	ext{des}}(z), \] 

where \( G_{\infty} \) is the bulk free energy (a constant that can be set to zero for the purpose of this problem).

\[\n\beta_{\text{eff}} = \beta_{0} + \alpha\,E ,\n\]

where β₀ is the intrinsic (field‑free) hyperpolarizability, α is the first‑order electric‑field‑induced hyperpolarizability, and E = V_m/d with V_m the membrane potential and d ≈ 5 nm the membrane thickness.

\[\nI_{2\omega}=K\Bigl[N\;\bigl\langle\beta_{\text{eff}}\cos\theta\bigr\rangle\Bigr]^{2} I_{\omega}^{2},\n\]

where K is a constant, I_ω is the incident fundamental intensity, and ⟨…⟩ denotes an ensemble average over the orientational distribution. The orientation distribution follows a Boltzmann factor with energy U(θ)=‑\mu E cosθ, where μ is the molecular dipole moment (in the direction of the principal axis) and the temperature is T = 300 K.

Assume that for the physiological range of membrane potentials (‑100 mV ≤ V_m ≤ +100 mV) the orientational distribution is only weakly perturbed, so that ⟨cosθ⟩ can be treated as a constant C₀.

(a) Derive an expression for the fractional change in SHG intensity, ΔI_{2ω}/I_{2ω}, produced by a small change in membrane potential ΔV_m (with ΔV_m ≪ V_m). Express your result in terms of β₀, α, d, C₀, and ΔV_m.
unverified_model_answer:
The SHG intensity for a monolayer of probes is  

\[
I_{2\omega}=K\Bigl[N\langle\beta_{\rm eff}\cos\theta\rangle\Bigr]^{2}I_{\omega}^{2}
      =K\Bigl[N\,C_{0}\bigl(\beta_{0}+\alpha E\bigr)\Bigr]^{2}I_{\omega}^{2},
\qquad 
E=\frac{V_{m}}{d}.
\]

Hence  

\[
I_{2\omega}=K N^{2}C_{0}^{2}\Bigl(\beta_{0}+\alpha\frac{V_{m}}{d}\Bigr)^{2} I_{\omega}^{2}.
\]

For a small change of the membrane potential, \(\Delta V_{m}\) (with \(\Delta V_{m}\ll V_{m}\)), expand to first order:

\[
\Delta I_{2\omega}
   \simeq \frac{dI_{2\omega}}{dV_{m}}\;\Delta V_{m}
   =K N^{2}C_{0}^{2}\,2\Bigl(\beta_{0}+\alpha\frac{V_{m}}{d}\Bigr)
      \Bigl(\frac{\alpha}{d}\Bigr)\Delta V_{m}\; I_{\omega}^{2}.
\]

Dividing by the original intensity gives the fractional change

\[
\frac{\Delta I_{2\omega}}{I_{2\omega}}
   \simeq \frac{2\alpha\Delta V_{m}}{d\Bigl(\beta_{0}+\alpha V_{m}/d\Bigr)}.
\]

Because the factor \(C_{0}\) (and the constants \(K,N,I_{\omega}\)) cancel, the fractional change does **not** depend on the orientational average under the stated approximations.  

If the field‑induced contribution is small \((\alpha V_{m}/d\ll\beta_{0})\), the denominator can be replaced by \(\beta_{0}\), yielding the simple linear relation  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\frac{\Delta I_{2\omega}}{I_{2\omega}}
   \;\approx\; \frac{2\alpha}{\beta_{0}d}\,\Delta V_{m}
}
\]

which is expressed solely in terms of the intrinsic hyperpolarizability \(\beta_{0}\), the field‑induced coefficient \(\alpha\), the membrane thickness \(d\), and the voltage change \(\Delta V_{m}\). (The constant orientational factor \(C_{0}\) cancels out.)

The side‑chain lengths studied experimentally are methyl (C₁), octyl (C₈), and dioctyl (C₈–C₈, i.e., two octyl groups per repeat unit). Each polymer film is cast onto a platinum substrate and used as the sensing membrane in an aqueous solution containing a monovalent chloride salt (e.g., NaCl).

The open‑circuit potential (OCP) of each ISE follows a **modified Nernst relationship**:

\[E = E^{\circ} +  rac{RT}{zF}\,\ln a_{	ext{M}^+} + \Delta E_{	ext{poly}}\]

where  

* \(E^{\circ}\) is a polymer‑independent reference term,
* \(z\) is the charge of the cation (here \(z = +1\)),
* \(a_{	ext{M}^+}\) is the activity of the monovalent cation,
* \(\Delta E_{	ext{poly}}\) is a polymer‑specific offset that accounts for incomplete charge compensation within the polymer matrix.

A simple thermodynamic model links \(\Delta E_{	ext{poly}}\) to the **effective charge‑transfer number** \(n_{	ext{eff}}\) of the membrane:

\[\Delta E_{	ext{poly}} =  rac{RT}{F}\,\ln\! igl(1- eta igr),\qquad 
n_{	ext{eff}} = z\,(1- eta)\]

The parameter \( eta\) (0 ≤ β < 1) quantifies the fraction of the membrane’s charge that is **screened** by neutral, non‑ionic polymer segments (i.e., the alkyl side chains). Empirically, \( eta\) has been found to increase linearly with the **normalized side‑chain volume** \(V_{	ext{norm}}\):

\[ eta = k\,V_{	ext{norm}},\qquad V_{	ext{norm}} =  rac{V_{	ext{side}}}{V_{	ext{repeat}}}\]

where  

* \(V_{	ext{side}}\) is the van‑der‑Waals volume of the side‑chain(s) per repeat unit,
* \(V_{	ext{repeat}} = 150\;	ext{Å}^3\) is the volume of the thiophene backbone plus a hydrogen atom (taken as constant for all polymers),
* \(k = 0.12\) (dimensionless) is a proportionality constant determined from independent swelling experiments.

The van‑der‑Waals volumes of the relevant alkyl groups are:  

| Alkyl group | \(V_{	ext{group}}\) (Å³) |
|-------------|--------------------------|
| CH₃         |  54                      |
| C₈H₁₇       |  250                     |
| (C₈H₁₇)₂    |  500                     |
| C₁₀H₂₁      |  320                     |

The experimentally measured **sensitivity slopes** (the change in OCP per decade change in cation activity) for the three polymers are:

| Polymer (side chain) | Measured slope (mV dec⁻¹) |
|----------------------|---------------------------|
| Methyl (C₁)          | 55                        |
| Octyl (C₈)           | 45                        |
| Dioctyl (C₈–C₈)      | 35                        |

All measurements were performed at 25 °C (298 K).

Task 1: Derive the theoretical expression for the slope (in mV dec⁻¹) of the OCP versus \log a_{	ext{M}^+} for these polymeric ISEs, explicitly showing how the slope depends on  eta (or equivalently on V_{	ext{norm}}).

\[
\boxed{%
S \;=\;\frac{2.303\,RT}{zF}\,(1-\beta)
      \;=\;\frac{2.303\,RT}{zF}\,\Bigl[1-k\,V_{\rm norm}\Bigr]
      \;=\;\frac{2.303\,RT}{zF}\,
        \Bigl[1-k\,\frac{V_{\rm side}}{V_{\rm repeat}}\Bigr]
      \;\;(\text{mV per decade})}
\]

At 25 °C ( \(T=298\) K) and for a monovalent ion (\(z=1\)), \(\frac{2.303RT}{F}=59.16\) mV, so the slope can be written as  

\[
\boxed{%
S\;\approx\;59.16\Bigl[1-k\,\frac{V_{\rm side}}{V_{\rm repeat}}\Bigr]\;\text{mV·dec}^{-1}}
\] 

or, using the normalized side‑chain volume \(V_{\rm norm}=V_{\rm side}/V_{\rm repeat}\),

\[
\boxed{%
S\;\approx\;59.16\,(1-k\,V_{\rm norm})\;\text{mV·dec}^{-1}}.
\]

Consider a one‑dimensional polymer consisting of *N* repeat units. Each repeat unit contains a conjugated diyne segment that contributes to an extended π‑electron system and a side‑chain bearing complementary hydrogen‑bonding groups. The polymer can adopt two idealized conformations:

1. **Linear (extended) conformation** – all dihedral angles between adjacent repeat units are ≈ 0°, allowing the side‑chains to form a regular hydrogen‑bonding network.
2. **Zig‑zag (folded) conformation** – each repeat unit is rotated by a fixed angle θ₀ (≈ 30°) relative to its neighbours, disrupting the hydrogen‑bonding network but relieving torsional strain.

The energetic model for the polymer is as follows:

* **Torsional energy:** Each dihedral angle θ contributes a harmonic penalty
  \[
  V_{\text{tor}}(\theta)=\tfrac12 k \theta^{2},
  \]
  where *k* is the torsional force constant (in J rad⁻²). In the linear conformation θ≈0, while in the zig‑zag conformation θ=θ₀ for every bond.

* **Hydrogen‑bonding energy:** In the linear conformation each repeat unit participates in one hydrogen bond of energy –ε (ε > 0). In the zig‑zag conformation these bonds are broken, giving zero hydrogen‑bond contribution.

* **Configurational entropy:** Treat each dihedral as an independent quantum harmonic oscillator with frequency ω = √(k/I) (I is the effective moment of inertia). The partition function for a single dihedral is
  \[
  Z_{\text{osc}}=\frac{e^{-\beta\hbar\omega/2}}{1-e^{-\beta\hbar\omega}},
  \]
  where β = 1/(k\_B T). The total entropy contribution for *N* dihedrals is S = N k_{\mathrm B}\,\ln Z_{\text{osc}} + N k_{\mathrm B}\,β\langle E_{\text{osc}}\rangle.

* **Electronic (optical) transition:** Approximate the π‑electron system as a particle in a one‑dimensional box of length *L*. For the linear conformation the conjugation length is L_{\text{lin}} = a N (a is the repeat‑unit length). In the folded conformation the effective conjugation is reduced by a fixed amount δ (δ ≈ 2a) because the rotation interrupts delocalisation, giving L_{\text{fold}} = a(N-\delta/a). The lowest allowed electronic transition energy is
  \[
  E_{1}= \frac{h^{2}}{8 m_{\mathrm e} L^{2}},
  \]
  and the corresponding absorption wavelength is \lambda = hc/E_{1}.

Task: Derive an expression for the Helmholtz free‑energy difference between the linear and folded conformations, ΔF(N)=F_{\text{fold}}(N)-F_{\text{lin}}(N), including (i) the total torsional energy, (ii) the total hydrogen‑bonding energy, and (iii) the entropic contribution from the harmonic‑oscillator model. Express ΔF(N) in terms of N, k, θ₀, ε, T, and the oscillator parameters.
unverified_model_answer:
The Helmholtz free energy of a given conformation is  

\[
F=U-TS=-k_{\mathrm B}T\ln Z_{\text{tot}},
\qquad 
Z_{\text{tot}}=Z_{\text{tor}}\,Z_{\text{HB}}\,Z_{\text{osc}}^{\,N}.
\]

* **Torsional (static) energy**  

\[
U_{\text{tor}}^{\text{lin}}=0 ,\qquad 
U_{\text{tor}}^{\text{fold}}=N\;\frac12 k\theta_{0}^{2}.
\]

* **Hydrogen‑bonding energy**  

\[
U_{\text{HB}}^{\text{lin}}=-N\varepsilon ,\qquad 
U_{\text{HB}}^{\text{fold}}=0 .
\]

* **Harmonic‑oscillator contribution**  

For one dihedral  

\[
Z_{\text{osc}}=\frac{e^{-\beta\hbar\omega/2}}{1-e^{-\beta\hbar\omega}},\qquad 
\langle E_{\text{osc}}\rangle=\hbar\omega\!\left(\frac12+\frac{1}{e^{\beta\hbar\omega}-1}\right),
\]

so that  

\[
S=N k_{\mathrm B}\Bigl[\ln Z_{\text{osc}}+\beta\langle E_{\text{osc}}\rangle\Bigr],
\qquad 
F_{\text{osc}}=-N k_{\mathrm B}T\ln Z_{\text{osc}} .
\]

Because the curvature of the torsional potential (the force constant \(k\)) and the moment of inertia \(I\) are the same in the two conformations, the oscillator frequency \(\omega=\sqrt{k/I}\) – and therefore \(Z_{\text{osc}}\) and \(\langle E_{\text{osc}}\rangle\) – are identical for the linear and the folded states. Consequently the entropic term cancels in the free‑energy difference.

Putting the contributions together:

\[
\begin{aligned}
F_{\text{lin}} &= -N\varepsilon -N k_{\mathrm B}T\ln Z_{\text{osc}},\\[4pt]
F_{\text{fold}}&= N\frac12 k\theta_{0}^{2} -N k_{\mathrm B}T\ln Z_{\text{osc}} .
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{\;\Delta F(N)=F_{\text{fold}}-F_{\text{lin}}
      =N\Bigl(\frac12 k\theta_{0}^{2}+\varepsilon\Bigr)\;}
\]

or, keeping the entropy term explicitly,

\[
\Delta F(N)=N\Bigl(\frac12 k\theta_{0}^{2}+\varepsilon\Bigr)
           -N k_{\mathrm B}T\Bigl[
               \ln\frac{Z_{\text{osc}}(\theta_{0})}{Z_{\text{osc}}(0)}
               +\beta\bigl(\langle E_{\text{osc}}\rangle_{\theta_{0}}
                         -\langle E_{\text{osc}}\rangle_{0}\bigr)
             \Bigr],
\]

with \(Z_{\text{osc}}=e^{-\beta\hbar\omega/2}/(1-e^{-\beta\hbar\omega})\) and  
\(\langle E_{\text{osc}}\rangle=\hbar\omega\bigl(\tfrac12+1/(e^{\beta\hbar\omega}-1)\bigr)\).

Since the oscillator partition function and average energy are independent of the equilibrium angle, the bracketed term vanishes, leaving the compact result shown in the boxed expression.

2. Oxidative addition of PhI to afford a square‑planar Pd(II) aryl‑iodide complex [Pd(NHC)₂(Ph)(I)].
3. Coordination of Acr to the Pd(II) centre, followed by migratory insertion to generate a Pd(II) alkyl‑aryl intermediate [Pd(NHC)₂(Ph‑CH₂‑CH₂‑CO₂Bu)].
4. β‑Hydride elimination to release the Heck product Ph‑CH=CH‑CO₂Bu and form a Pd(II)‑hydride [Pd(NHC)₂(H)(I)].
5. Reductive elimination (or base‑mediated removal of HI) to regenerate the active Pd(0) species and close the cycle.

(e) The experimentally measured TOF for the original NHC system at 80 °C is 120 h⁻¹. Assuming that the rate‑determining step is β‑hydride elimination (step 4) and that it follows simple first‑order kinetics with a pre‑exponential factor A = 1 × 10¹³ s⁻¹, estimate the activation free energy ΔG‡ for this step. Show all steps of your calculation (convert TOF to s⁻¹, use the Eyring equation, etc.).

**Step 1 – Convert the TOF to a first‑order rate constant**

\[
\text{TOF}=120\;\text{h}^{-1}
          =\frac{120}{3600}\;\text{s}^{-1}
          =3.33\times10^{-2}\;\text{s}^{-1}=k
\]

**Step 2 – Write the Eyring equation**

\[
k=\frac{k_{\rm B}T}{h}\;e^{-\Delta G^{\ddagger}/RT}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\Delta G^{\ddagger}=-RT\ln\!\left(\frac{k\,h}{k_{\rm B}T}\right)
\]

where  

\(k_{\rm B}=1.3806\times10^{-23}\;{\rm J\,K^{-1}}\)  

\(h=6.6261\times10^{-34}\;{\rm J\,s}\)  

\(R=8.314\;{\rm J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}\)  

\(T=80^{\circ}{\rm C}=353\;{\rm K}\).

**Step 3 – Evaluate the pre‑exponential term**

\[
\frac{k_{\rm B}T}{h}= \frac{(1.3806\times10^{-23})(353)}{6.6261\times10^{-34}}
                     =7.36\times10^{12}\;{\rm s^{-1}}
\]

\[
\frac{k\,h}{k_{\rm B}T}= \frac{3.33\times10^{-2}}{7.36\times10^{12}}
                        =4.53\times10^{-15}
\]

\[
\ln\!\left(\frac{k\,h}{k_{\rm B}T}\right)=\ln(4.53\times10^{-15})=-33.03
\]

\[
\Delta G^{\ddagger}= - (8.314\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1})(353\;\text{K})(-33.03)
                    =9.70\times10^{4}\;\text{J mol}^{-1}

\[

   where *A*ₐₚ is the aperture area, *k*ᴮ is Boltzmann’s constant, and *m*ₕ₂ is the mass of an H₂ molecule.

   \[ k_{\text{out}} = \nu \exp\!\left(-\frac{E_{a}}{RT}\right), \]
   where *ν* is the pre‑exponential factor (≈ 10¹³ s⁻¹) and *R* is the gas constant.

      \frac{P}{k_{\rm B}T}}
      {\displaystyle 
      \gamma A_{\rm ap}\sqrt{\frac{k_{\rm B}T}{2\pi m_{\rm H_2}}}\,
      \frac{P}{k_{\rm B}T}

\]

\]

A liquid electrolyte contains the redox couple Fe(CN)₆³⁻ / Fe(CN)₆⁴⁻ with a fixed total concentration

1. **Ps formation** \( P \xrightarrow{k_f\,C_{\text{tot}}} \text{Ps} \) (rate constant \(k_f\) [M⁻¹ s⁻¹]),  
2. **Quenching of Ps formation** by the two ions:  

   \[
   P + \text{Fe(CN)}_6^{3-} \xrightarrow{k_{q3}} \text{no\,Ps},
   \qquad
   P + \text{Fe(CN)}_6^{4-} \xrightarrow{k_{q4}} \text{no\,Ps},
   \]

   with rate constants \(k_{q3},k_{q4}\) [M⁻¹ s⁻¹],  
3. **Oxidation of Ps** by Fe(CN)₆³⁻: \( \text{Ps} + \text{Fe(CN)}_6^{3-} \xrightarrow{k_{\text{ox}}} \text{annihilation} \) (rate constant \(k_{\text{ox}}\) [s⁻¹]),  
4. **Intrinsic annihilation** of Ps with rate \(k_{\text{a}}\) [s⁻¹] (take \(k_{\text{a}}=1/τ_0\) with the vacuum Ps lifetime \(τ_0≈0.5\) ns).  

A constant positron injection rate \(I\) (positrons s⁻¹) is maintained by the source.  

During a cyclic voltammetry (CV) experiment the electrode potential is swept linearly in time,

\[
E(t)=E_{\text{init}}+\nu t,
\]

with scan rate \(\nu\) (V s⁻¹). Electron transfer at the electrode is assumed fast, so that at any instant the ion concentrations obey the Nernst relation

\[
\frac{[\text{Fe(CN)}_6^{3-}]}{[\text{Fe(CN)}_6^{4-}]}
=
\exp\!\Bigl[\frac{F}{RT}\bigl(E(t)-E^{0}\bigr)\Bigr]
\equiv r(t),
\]

where \(E^{0}\) is the standard redox potential, \(F\) Faraday’s constant, \(R\) the gas constant and \(T\) the temperature.

---

### (a) Kinetic equations

-\;k_f\,C_{\rm tot}\,P
-\;k_{q3}\,[\text{Fe(CN)}_6^{3-}]\,P
-\;k_{q4}\,[\text{Fe(CN)}_6^{4-}]\,P,\\[4pt]
\frac{d\text{Ps}}{dt}&=k_f\,C_{\rm tot}\,P
-\;\Big(k_{\rm ox}\,[\text{Fe(CN)}_6^{3-}]+k_{\rm a}\Big)\,\text{Ps},

Consider a polyatomic molecule that contains a carbonyl (C=O) group and a hydroxyl (–OH) group attached to the same carbon skeleton (e.g., a carboxylic acid or an ester). A metastable rare‑gas atom in the 2³S state (ionization energy 19.8 eV) collides with this molecule at translational energies ranging from 0.1 eV to 2.0 eV, leading to Penning ionization and the ejection of an electron.

(a) Derive the relationship between the kinetic energy of the emitted electron E_e and the collision energy E_{\text{col}} for Penning ionization, taking into account the internal excitation (vibrational/rotational) of the ionized fragment.
unverified_model_answer:
**Derivation**

For a Penning‐ionization event  

\[
\mathrm{RG}^{*}(2^{3}S)+\mathrm{M}\;\longrightarrow\;\mathrm{RG}+ \mathrm{M}^{+}+e^{-},
\]

energy conservation gives  

\[
E_{\text{int}}(\mathrm{RG}^{*})+E_{\text{col}}+E_{\text{int}}(\mathrm{M})
= I_{\mathrm{M}}+E_{e}+E_{\text{int}}(\mathrm{M}^{+})+E_{\text{recoil}},
\]

where  

* \(E_{\text{int}}(\mathrm{RG}^{*})\) – internal (excitation) energy of the metastable rare‑gas atom (for He(2³S) ≈ 19.8 eV);  
* \(E_{\text{col}}\) – translational collision energy;  
* \(I_{\mathrm{M}}\) – ionization energy of the neutral molecule (≈ 10–12 eV for a carboxylic acid or ester);  
* \(E_{\text{int}}(\mathrm{M}^{+})\) – internal (vibrational + rotational) excitation energy of the ion;  
* \(E_{\text{recoil}}\) – kinetic energy taken up by the heavy ion recoil (usually ≤ 0.1 eV and often neglected).

Re‑arranging for the kinetic energy of the emitted electron yields  

\[
E_{e}=E_{\text{int}}(\mathrm{RG}^{*})+E_{\text{col}}-I_{\mathrm{M}}
        -E_{\text{int}}(\mathrm{M}^{+})-E_{\text{recoil}} .
\]

If the recoil term is omitted (its contribution is small compared with the electron energy), the relationship simplifies to a linear dependence on the collision energy:

\[
\boxed{ \;E_{e}=E_{\text{col}}+\bigl(E_{\text{exc}}-I_{\mathrm{M}}\bigr)-E_{\text{vib/rot}}^{+}\; } 
\]

with  

* \(E_{\text{exc}}=19.8\;\text{eV}\) (the excitation energy of the 2³S metastable atom),  
* \(E_{\text{vib/rot}}^{+}\equiv E_{\text{int}}(\mathrm{M}^{+})\) the sum of vibrational and rotational quanta populated in the ion.

Thus the electron kinetic energy grows linearly with the collision energy, the intercept being the excess of the metastable internal energy over the molecular ionization energy, reduced by any internal excitation of the ionized fragment.

T0        | 350 K                         | 300 K

γ         | +1.0×10^10 J·m^9·C^{-6}        | +1.2×10^10 J·m^9·C^{-6}
Specific heat at constant field, C_E | 3.0×10^6 J·m^{-3} K^{-1} (assumed equal for both phases) | Same as orthorhombic

\]

In a rigid polymer matrix, acceptor molecules **A** are incorporated at a molar concentration c_A (mol L⁻¹) and are assumed to be randomly and homogeneously distributed. Energy transfer from the donor triplet state to the acceptor can proceed by two mechanisms:

1. **Förster (dipole‑dipole) transfer**, characterized by a Förster radius R₀ (the donor‑acceptor separation at which the transfer rate equals the donor’s intrinsic decay rate).
2. **Dexter (exchange) transfer**, which requires orbital overlap and is diffusion‑controlled in solution, with a bimolecular rate constant k_Dex (L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹).

Assume that in the solid polymer matrix the molecular diffusion is essentially frozen, so Dexter transfer can be neglected, whereas in a dilute solution both mechanisms are operative.

**Part A – Förster Transfer in a Rigid Matrix**

1. Derive an expression for the donor’s observed decay rate k_obs (s⁻¹) in the polymer matrix in terms of τ_D⁰, R₀, and c_A, assuming that each donor experiences a Poisson‑distributed number of acceptors within the Förster sphere of radius R₀.
unverified_model_answer:
In the rigid polymer matrix the acceptors are frozen in space.  
Let  

\[
k_0=\frac{1}{\tau_D^{0}}
\]

be the intrinsic donor decay rate.  
For a donor the average number of acceptors that lie inside a sphere of radius \(R_0\) (the Förster sphere) is  

\[
\lambda = \langle N\rangle = n_A V_{R_0}=c_A N_{\!A}\,\frac{4\pi}{3}R_0^{3},
\]

where \(n_A=c_A N_{\!A}\) is the number density of acceptors (molecules L\(^{-1}\)) and \(V_{R_0}=4\pi R_0^{3}/3\) is the sphere volume.

Because the donors and acceptors are randomly placed, the number of acceptors in the Förster sphere follows a Poisson distribution  

\[
P(N=n)=\frac{\lambda^{n}e^{-\lambda}}{n!}\, .
\]

If a donor has \(n\) acceptors within \(R_0\), each acceptor can receive energy with a Förster rate equal (by definition of \(R_0\)) to the intrinsic rate \(k_0\).  Hence the total decay rate for that donor is  

\[
k(n)=k_0 + n\,k_0 = k_0(1+n).
\]

The ensemble‑averaged (observed) decay rate is therefore  

\[
\begin{aligned}
k_{\text{obs}} &= \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}P(N=n)\,k(n)\\
&= k_0\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}P(N=n)(1+n)\\
&= k_0\bigl[1+\langle N\rangle\bigr] \\
&= k_0\Bigl[1+\lambda\Bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]

Substituting \(\lambda\) gives  

\[
\boxed{\,k_{\text{obs}}=\frac{1}{\tau_D^{0}}\left[1+\frac{4\pi}{3}\,N_{\!A}\,c_A\,R_0^{3}\right]\,}.
\]

Thus the donor’s observed decay rate in the rigid polymer matrix is the intrinsic rate multiplied by a factor that accounts for the average number of acceptors inside the Förster sphere.

Consider a family of donor–π–acceptor (D‑π‑A) styryl dyes can adopt two distinct ground‑state conformations:

* Conformer P (planar) – the donor and acceptor are coplanar, giving rise to a locally excited (LE) state upon photo‑excitation.
* Conformer T (twisted) – the donor is rotated relative to the acceptor, enabling formation of a twisted intramolecular charge‑transfer (TICT) state after excitation.

In a polar solvent the two conformers are in rapid thermal equilibrium in the ground state, with a free‑energy difference

\[\n\Delta G_{0}=G_{T}^{0}-G_{P}^{0}= -RT\ln K_{\text{eq}},\qquad K_{\text{eq}}=\frac{[T]}{[P]} .\n\]

Both conformers can be selectively excited at different wavelengths (\lambda_{ex}^{P} and \lambda_{ex}^{T}), but under broadband excitation both are populated. After excitation, the following processes compete (all rates are first‑order):

| Process | Rate constant |
|---|---|
| Radiative decay from LE (P*) | k_{r}^{\text{LE}} |
| Non‑radiative decay from LE (P*) | k_{nr}^{\text{LE}} |
| Radiative decay from TICT (T*) | k_{r}^{\text{TICT}} |
| Non‑radiative decay from TICT (T*) | k_{nr}^{\text{TICT}} |
| Excited‑state interconversion P* → T* | k_{PT} |
| Excited‑state interconversion T* → P* | k_{TP} |

Assume that intersystem crossing and other pathways are negligible.

**Task:** Derive the steady‑state populations of the excited states P* and T* under continuous excitation at a wavelength that excites both conformers proportionally to their ground‑state fractions. Express the steady‑state concentrations [P^{*}]_{ss} and [T^{*}]_{ss} in terms of the excitation rate I (photons·L^{-1}·s^{-1}), the ground‑state equilibrium constant K_{\text{eq}}, and the rate constants listed above.
unverified_model_answer:
The two ground‑state conformers are in equilibrium  

\[
K_{\rm eq}=\frac{[T]}{[P]},\qquad 
[P]+[T]=[D]_{\rm tot}\;( {\rm constant}) .
\]

A broadband beam of intensity \(I\;({\rm photons\,L^{-1}s^{-1}})\) excites each conformer in proportion to its ground‑state fraction, therefore  

\[
\begin{aligned}
R_{P}&={\rm formation\;rate\;of\;}P^{*}=I\,\frac{[P]}{[P]+[T]}
      =\frac{I}{1+K_{\rm eq}},\\[4pt]
R_{T}&={\rm formation\;rate\;of\;}T^{*}=I\,\frac{[T]}{[P]+[T]}
      =\frac{I\,K_{\rm eq}}{1+K_{\rm eq}} .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### Kinetic scheme for the excited states  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d[P^{*}]}{dt}&=R_{P}
-\bigl(k_{r}^{\rm LE}+k_{nr}^{\rm LE}+k_{PT}\bigr)[P^{*}]
+k_{TP}[T^{*}],\\[4pt]
\frac{d[T^{*}]}{dt}&=R_{T}
-\bigl(k_{r}^{\rm TICT}+k_{nr}^{\rm TICT}+k_{TP}\bigr)[T^{*}]
+k_{PT}[P^{*}].
\end{aligned}
\]

Introduce the total first‑order loss rates  

\[
k_{P}=k_{r}^{\rm LE}+k_{nr}^{\rm LE}+k_{PT},\qquad
k_{T}=k_{r}^{\rm TICT}+k_{nr}^{\rm TICT}+k_{TP}.
\]

At steady state \((d[P^{*}]/dt=d[T^{*}]/dt=0)\) :

\[
\begin{cases}
0=R_{P}-k_{P}[P^{*}]+k_{TP}[T^{*}],\\[4pt]
0=R_{T}-k_{T}[T^{*}]+k_{PT}[P^{*}].
\end{cases}
\]

These linear equations give  

\[
\begin{aligned}
[P^{*}]_{\rm ss}&=\frac{k_{T}R_{P}+k_{TP}R_{T}}{k_{P}k_{T}-k_{PT}k_{TP}},\\[4pt]
[T^{*}]_{\rm ss}&=\frac{k_{P}R_{T}+k_{PT}R_{P}}{k_{P}k_{T}-k_{PT}k_{TP}} .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### Substituting the excitation rates  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
[P^{*}]_{\rm ss}&=
\frac{I}{1+K_{\rm eq}}\;
\frac{k_{T}+K_{\rm eq}\,k_{TP}}
{(k_{r}^{\rm LE}+k_{nr}^{\rm LE}+k_{PT})
 \,(k_{r}^{\rm TICT}+k_{nr}^{\rm TICT}+k_{TP})-k_{PT}k_{TP}},\\[8pt]
[T^{*}]_{\rm ss}&=
\frac{I}{1+K_{\rm eq}}\;
\frac{K_{\rm eq}\,k_{P}+k_{PT}}
{(k_{r}^{\rm LE}+k_{nr}^{\rm LE}+k_{PT})
 \,(k_{r}^{\rm TICT}+k_{nr}^{\rm TICT}+k_{TP})-k_{PT}k_{TP}} .
\end{aligned}}
\]

where  

\[
k_{P}=k_{r}^{\rm LE}+k_{nr}^{\rm LE}+k_{PT},
\qquad
k_{T}=k_{r}^{\rm TICT}+k_{nr}^{\rm TICT}+k_{TP}.
\]

Equivalently, after expanding the numerators,

\[
\begin{aligned}
[P^{*}]_{\rm ss}&=
\frac{I}{1+K_{\rm eq}}\;
\frac{k_{r}^{\rm TICT}+k_{nr}^{\rm TICT}+k_{TP}(1+K_{\rm eq})}
{(k_{r}^{\rm LE}+k_{nr}^{\rm LE}+k_{PT})
 (k_{r}^{\rm TICT}+k_{nr}^{\rm TICT}+k_{TP})-k_{PT}k_{TP}},\\[6pt]
[T^{*}]_{\rm ss}&=
\frac{I}{1+K_{\rm eq}}\;
\frac{K_{\rm eq}(k_{r}^{\rm LE}+k_{nr}^{\rm LE})+k_{PT}(1+K_{\rm eq})}
{(k_{r}^{\rm LE}+k_{nr}^{\rm LE}+k_{PT})
 (k_{r}^{\rm TICT}+k_{nr}^{\rm TICT}+k_{TP})-k_{PT}k_{TP}} .
\end{aligned}
\]

These expressions give the steady‑state concentrations of the planar (LE) and twisted (TICT) excited states under broadband excitation, in terms of the excitation rate \(I\), the ground‑state equilibrium constant \(K_{\rm eq}\), and the kinetic constants of the system.

	ext{NaH}_{2}	ext{PO}_{4(g)} + 	ext{Zeolite(s)} \;\longrightarrow\; 	ext{NaH}_{2}	ext{PO}_{4}\!\-\!	ext{Zeolite(s)}
\]

\[
\Delta E_{	ext{ads}}(X)= -31.64\ 	ext{kJ mol}^{-1},\qquad 
\Delta E_{	ext{ads}}(Y)= -161\ 	ext{kJ mol}^{-1}.
\]

Assume that (i) the adsorption follows a Langmuir isotherm, (ii) the monolayer saturation capacity $q_{\max}$ is the same for both zeolites, and (iii) the Gibbs free energy change for adsorption can be approximated by the DFT adsorption energy (i.e., $\Delta G_{	ext{ads}}\approx\Delta E_{	ext{ads}}$).

The solution in which adsorption takes place is at 298 K and pH = 7.0, where the dominant phosphate species is H₂PO₄⁻ (the second dissociation constant of phosphoric acid is $pK_{a2}=7.2$). The surface acidity of the zeolite is governed by the Si/Al ratio: a lower Si/Al ratio yields a higher concentration of Brønsted acid sites (protonated framework oxygens), whereas a higher Si/Al ratio gives a more basic (alkaline) surface.

(a) Derive the Langmuir equilibrium constant K for each zeolite from the given adsorption energies.

The Langmuir equilibrium constant \(K\) is related to the standard free‑energy change for adsorption by  

\[
\Delta G_{\text{ads}}=-RT\ln K\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
K=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\Delta G_{\text{ads}}}{RT}\right).
\]

With the approximation \(\Delta G_{\text{ads}}\approx\Delta E_{\text{ads}}\) and using  
\(R=8.314\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\) and \(T=298\;\text{K}\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
K_X &=\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{-31.64\times10^{3}\;\text{J mol}^{-1}}{8.314\times298}\Bigr)
     =\exp\!\Bigl(\frac{31.64\times10^{3}}{2.477\times10^{3}}\Bigr)
     =\exp(12.78)\;\approx\;3.5\times10^{5},\\[4pt]
K_Y &=\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{-161\times10^{3}\;\text{J mol}^{-1}}{8.314\times298}\Bigr)
     =\exp\!\Bigl(\frac{161\times10^{3}}{2.477\times10^{3}}\Bigr)
     =\exp(64.97)\;\approx\;1.6\times10^{28}.
\end{aligned}
\]

\[
\boxed{K_X\;\approx\;3.5\times10^{5}\;\text{(M}^{-1}\text{)},\qquad 
       K_Y\;\approx\;1.6\times10^{28}\;\text{(M}^{-1}\text{)}}
\]

Solve the following problem. Make sure to put the answer (and only answer) inside  oxed{}.

A one‑dimensional transition‑metal oxide nanowire catalyst (core) has the following properties:

- Core material: α‑MnO₂
- Diameter of the core, \(d_{0}=20\ \text{nm}\)
- Length, \(L=2\ \mu\text{m}\)
- Intrinsic electronic conductivity of the core, \(\sigma_{0}=3.2\times10^{-6}\ \text{S·cm}^{-1}\)

The nanowire is uniformly coated with an amorphous carbon shell:

- Shell thickness, \(t=5\ \text{nm}\) (so the total outer diameter is \(d = d_{0}+2t\))
- Conductivity of the carbon shell, \(\sigma_{\text{C}}=1000\ \text{S·cm}^{-1}\) (typical for disordered carbon)
- The carbon mass fraction in the composite is \(\le 1.2\%\) (i.e., the coating is very thin and low‑mass).

Electrochemical measurements for the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) on the nanowire electrode are interpreted with a Randles equivalent circuit, where the charge‑transfer resistance is

\[R_{\text{ct}}=\frac{RT}{nF\,i_{0}}\]

with the exchange current density approximated by

\[i_{0}\propto \sigma_{\text{eff}}\;A_{\text{s}}\;\theta_{\text{Mn}^{3+}}\]

Here

- \(\sigma_{\text{eff}}\) is the effective electronic conductivity of the core‑shell nanowire,
- \(A_{\text{s}}\) is the electrochemically active surface area of the nanowire (assume the entire outer surface is active),
- \(\theta_{\text{Mn}^{3+}}\) is the surface fraction of Mn\(^{3+}\) active sites, which increases from \(\theta_{0}=0.12\) (bare MnO₂) to \(\theta_{1}=0.25\) after carbon coating.

The experimentally measured charge‑transfer resistance decreases from \(R_{\text{ct},0}=6.2\ \text{k}\Omega\) (bare nanowire) to \(R_{\text{ct},1}=0.9\ \text{k}\Omega\) (carbon‑coated nanowire).

**Task:**

(a) Derive an expression for the effective longitudinal conductivity \(\sigma_{\text{eff}}\) of the core‑shell nanowire assuming the current flows parallel to the nanowire axis and that the core and shell conduct in parallel (i.e., the total conductance is the sum of the conductances of core and shell).
unverified_model_answer:
The longitudinal conductance of a cylindrical wire is  

\[
G=\frac{\sigma A}{L},
\]

where \(A\) is the cross‑sectional area normal to the current flow.  
For a core–shell nanowire the core (radius \(r_{0}=d_{0}/2\)) and the carbon shell (outer radius \(r=r_{0}+t\)) conduct **in parallel**, so the total conductance is the sum of the individual conductances:

\[
G_{\text{tot}}=G_{\text{core}}+G_{\text{shell}}
           =\frac{\sigma_{0}\,A_{\text{core}}}{L}+\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm C}\,A_{\text{shell}}}{L}.
\]

Here  

\[
A_{\text{core}}=\pi r_{0}^{2},\qquad 
A_{\text{shell}}=\pi\bigl(r^{2}-r_{0}^{2}\bigr),\qquad 
A_{\text{tot}}=\pi r^{2}.
\]

Define an **effective conductivity** \(\sigma_{\text{eff}}\) for the whole nanowire by  

\[
G_{\text{tot}}=\frac{\sigma_{\text{eff}}\,A_{\text{tot}}}{L}.
\]

Equating the two expressions for \(G_{\text{tot}}\) and cancelling the common factor \(\pi/L\) gives  

\[
\sigma_{\text{eff}}\,r^{2}= \sigma_{0}\,r_{0}^{2}+ \sigma_{\mathrm C}\,\bigl(r^{2}-r_{0}^{2}\bigr).
\]

Hence  

\[
\boxed{\;
\sigma_{\text{eff}}=
\frac{\sigma_{0}\,r_{0}^{2}+\sigma_{\mathrm C}\,\bigl(r^{2}-r_{0}^{2}\bigr)}{r^{2}}
= \sigma_{0}\left(\frac{r_{0}}{r}\right)^{2}
  +\sigma_{\mathrm C}\Bigl[1-\left(\frac{r_{0}}{r}\right)^{2}\Bigr]
\;}
\]

or, expressed in terms of the diameters,

\[
\boxed{\;
\sigma_{\text{eff}}=
\sigma_{0}\left(\frac{d_{0}}{d_{0}+2t}\right)^{2}
+\sigma_{\mathrm C}\left[1-\left(\frac{d_{0}}{d_{0}+2t}\right)^{2}\right].
\;}
\]

Consider a biradical molecule that contains two localized spin‑½ centers (denoted A and B) connected through a non‑conjugated three‑carbon bridge (C–C–C). The geometry is such that the singly‑occupied molecular orbitals (SOMOs) on A and B are oriented perpendicular to the plane of the bridge, and the bridge itself does not possess an extended π‑system. The relevant structural and electronic parameters are:
* Distance A–B = 3.5 Å.
* Distance from each radical center to the nearest bridge carbon = 1.45 Å.
* The bridge provides a σ‑bonding orbital (energy ε_σ = –0.8 eV) and a σ*‑antibonding orbital (energy ε_σ* = +0.6 eV).
* Overlap integrals between each SOMO and the σ orbital: S = 0.07; between each SOMO and the σ* orbital: S' = 0.03.
* On‑site Coulomb repulsion (Hubbard U) for each radical: U = 3.5 eV.
* Electron‑transfer (hopping) integral between a SOMO and a bridge orbital can be approximated as t = β S (or t' = β S') with β = –2.5 eV.

Assume that the dominant magnetic exchange mechanism is superexchange mediated by virtual electron transfer through the σ and σ* bridge orbitals.

---

**(a) Superexchange derivation and numerical evaluation**
Using second‑order perturbation theory for the superexchange mechanism, derive an expression for the isotropic Heisenberg exchange constant J (in cm⁻¹) that includes contributions from both the σ and σ* pathways. Show that, to leading order,

J \approx -\frac{2}{U}\left(\frac{t^{2}}{\Delta_{\sigma}} + \frac{t'^{2}}{\Delta_{\sigma^{*}}}\right),

where \Delta_{\sigma}= \varepsilon_{\sigma} - \varepsilon_{\text{SOMO}} and \Delta_{\sigma^{*}}= \varepsilon_{\sigma^{*}} - \varepsilon_{\text{SOMO}}. Take the SOMO energy as the reference (0 eV). Evaluate J numerically with the data given, and convert the result to cm⁻¹ (use 1 eV = 8065.54 cm⁻¹).

The superexchange interaction between the two spin‑½ radicals can be treated with Anderson’s second‑order perturbation theory.  
For a virtual hop of an electron from a SOMO on site \(A\) (or \(B\)) onto a bridge orbital \(\mu\) (σ or σ*), and back onto the opposite radical, the intermediate state has a doubly‑occupied radical with an energy penalty \(U\) and an orbital‑energy denominator \(\Delta_{\mu}= \varepsilon_{\mu}-\varepsilon_{\text{SOMO}}\).  Projecting the fourth‑order hopping process onto the low‑energy spin subspace yields the isotropic Heisenberg Hamiltonian  

\[
\hat H = J\,\mathbf S_A\!\cdot\!\mathbf S_B ,
\qquad 
J = -\,\frac{2}{U}\sum_{\mu=\sigma,\sigma^{*}}\frac{t_{\mu}^{2}}{\Delta_{\mu}} .
\]

Here the factor 2 comes from the two possible sequences of hops (A→bridge→B and B→bridge→A).  

---

### Numerical evaluation  

The hopping integrals are obtained from the overlap integrals:

\[
t = \beta S = (-2.5\;\text{eV})(0.07) = -0.175\;\text{eV},
\qquad
t' = \beta S' = (-2.5\;\text{eV})(0.03) = -0.075\;\text{eV}.
\]

With the SOMO taken as the zero of energy,

\[
\Delta_{\sigma}= \varepsilon_{\sigma}-\varepsilon_{\text{SOMO}} = -0.8\;\text{eV},
\qquad
\Delta_{\sigma^{*}}= \varepsilon_{\sigma^{*}}-\varepsilon_{\text{SOMO}} = +0.6\;\text{eV}.
\]

Hence

\[
\frac{t^{2}}{\Delta_{\sigma}} = \frac{(-0.175)^{2}}{-0.8}
   = -0.03828\;\text{eV},
\qquad
\frac{t'^{2}}{\Delta_{\sigma^{*}}}= \frac{(-0.075)^{2}}{+0.6}
   = +0.00938\;\text{eV}.
\]

The sum of the two pathways is  

\[
\frac{t^{2}}{\Delta_{\sigma}}+\frac{t'^{2}}{\Delta_{\sigma^{*}}}
   = -0.02891\;\text{eV}.
\]

Finally,

\[
J = -\frac{2}{U}\Bigl(-0.02891\Bigr)
    = \frac{2}{3.5}\,(0.02891)
    = 0.0165\;\text{eV}.
\]

Converting to wavenumbers ( \(1\;\text{eV}=8065.54\;\text{cm}^{-1}\) ):

\[
J = 0.0165\;\text{eV}\times 8065.54\;\frac{\text{cm}^{-1}}{\text{eV}}
    \approx 1.33\times10^{2}\;\text{cm}^{-1}.
\]

\boxed{133\ \text{cm}^{-1}}

\[

&\approx 1.69\times10^{10},
\end{aligned}
\]

\[
\ln\!\left(\frac{k_{\mathrm B}T}{hk}\right)=\ln(1.69\times10^{10})\approx 23.55.
\]

\[

                     \approx 64\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}.
\]

Consider a nanosecond‑scale pulsed dielectric‑barrier discharge (DBD) operated in a flowing mixture of ethylene (C₂H₄), oxygen (O₂), and argon (Ar) at reduced pressure. The discharge is modeled with a one‑dimensional (1‑D) fluid description that couples the electron continuity, momentum, and energy equations to Poisson’s equation, and incorporates a detailed plasma‑chemical kinetic mechanism (including electron‑impact dissociation, excitation, ionization, and subsequent neutral reactions). The applied voltage pulse has peak amplitude V₀ and duration τₚ, delivering an energy per pulse E_in. Assume the electron energy distribution function (EEDF) can be approximated locally by a Maxwellian with temperature T_e(x), and that the reduced electric field E/N varies spatially due to sheath formation.

(Derivation of power deposition) Derive an expression for the local volumetric power density P_e(x) deposited into electron‑impact processes in terms of the local reduced electric field (E/N)(x), electron density n_e(x), electron mobility μ_e(x), and any other necessary transport coefficients. Clearly state any assumptions made (e.g., neglect of electron diffusion, steady‑state electron energy balance).
unverified_model_answer:
**Derivation (outline).**  

1. **Electron current density.**  
   With drift‐dominated transport and neglect of diffusion, the electron current density is  

   \[
   \mathbf{J}_e(x)= -e\,n_e(x)\,\mu_e(x)\,\mathbf{E}(x) ,
   \qquad 
   \sigma(x)=e\,n_e(x)\,\mu_e(x)
   \]

   where \(e\) is the elementary charge, \(n_e\) the electron density, \(\mu_e\) the electron mobility, and \(\mathbf{E}\) the electric field.

2. **Power transferred from the field to the electrons.**  
   The volumetric Joule heating (power per unit volume) is  

   \[
   P_{\text{Joule}}(x)=\mathbf{J}_e\!\cdot\!\mathbf{E}= \sigma(x)\,E^2(x)
   =e\,n_e(x)\,\mu_e(x)\,E^2(x).
   \]

3. **Steady‑state electron‑energy balance.**  
   Assuming a steady‑state electron energy equation and that the electron energy gained from the field is lost exclusively by electron‑impact (inelastic) collisions (elastic heating is negligible at the low pressures of nanosecond DBDs),

   \[
   P_e(x)=P_{\text{Joule}}(x).
   \]

   Hence the local power density deposited into electron‑impact processes equals the Joule heating term.

4. **Expressing through the reduced electric field.**  
   The reduced electric field is defined as  

   \[
   \frac{E}{N}(x)=\frac{E(x)}{N},
   \]

   where \(N\) is the neutral gas number density (assumed spatially uniform for a given pressure). Therefore  

   \[
   E(x)=N\;\Bigl(\frac{E}{N}\Bigr)(x).
   \]

   Substituting this into the Joule term gives  

   \[
   P_e(x)=e\,n_e(x)\,\mu_e(x)\,\big[N\,(E/N)(x)\big]^2
        =e\,n_e(x)\,\mu_e(x)\,N^{2}\,\Bigl[\frac{E}{N}(x)\Bigr]^{2}.
   \]

5. **Alternative form using an energy‑loss function.**  
   If one wishes to write the power directly as the sum of all inelastic losses, an energy‑loss function \(L(E/N)\) can be introduced:

   \[
   P_e(x)=n_e(x)\,L\!\bigl[(E/N)(x)\bigr],
   \qquad

A cooled semibatch reactor is used for a liquid‑liquid exothermic reaction in which a feed of reactant **A** (mol s⁻¹) is introduced continuously into a well‑mixed liquid phase that already contains reactant **B**. The two liquids are immiscible, and mass transfer of **A** across the interface controls the availability of **A** for reaction.

The governing equations are:

1. **Mass balance for A in the reacting phase**
\[\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(V C_A\bigr)=F - J\,V,\qquad J = k_{L}a\bigl(C_A^{*}-C_A\bigr),\]
where
- \(V(t)\) is the reactor volume (assume constant density, so \(V\) grows only due to the feed),
- \(C_A(t)\) is the concentration of A in the reacting phase,
- \(F\) (mol s⁻¹) is the molar feed rate of A,
- \(k_{L}a\) (s⁻¹) is the overall liquid‑phase mass‑transfer coefficient,
- \(C_A^{*}=K\,C_B\) is the equilibrium concentration of A in the reacting phase, with \(K\) the distribution coefficient (dimensionless) and \(C_B\) the (assumed constant) concentration of B in the non‑reacting phase.

2. **Reaction rate**
The intrinsic (chemical) rate law is first‑order in A:
\[r_{\text{chem}} = k_0 \exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{E_a}{RT}\Bigr) C_A,\]
with pre‑exponential factor \(k_0\) (s⁻¹), activation energy \(E_a\) (J mol⁻¹), gas constant \(R\), and temperature \(T\) (K).
Because the reaction is “fast” and mass‑transfer limited, the *effective* rate is the smaller of the chemical rate and the mass‑transfer flux per unit volume:
\[r_{\text{eff}} = \min\bigl(r_{\text{chem}},\,J\bigr).\]
In the fast‑reaction regime the effective activation energy is observed to be halved, i.e. \(E_a^{\text{eff}} = \tfrac{1}{2}E_a\).

3. **Energy balance**
\[\rho C_p V \frac{dT}{dt}= -U A\,(T-T_c) + (-\Delta H)\,V\,r_{\text{eff}},\]
where \(\rho\) (kg m⁻³) and \(C_p\) (J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) are the density and heat capacity of the reacting mixture, \(U A\) (W K⁻¹) is the overall heat‑removal coefficient to a coolant at temperature \(T_c\) (K), and \(-\Delta H\) (J mol⁻¹) is the (positive) heat of reaction.

Assume the following numerical data (all constants are temperature‑independent unless otherwise noted):

| Parameter | Symbol | Value |
|-----------|--------|-------|
| Feed rate of A | \(F\) | variable (mol s⁻¹) |
| Initial reactor volume | \(V_0\) | 0.10 m³ |
| Density | \(\rho\) | 1000 kg m⁻³ |
| Heat capacity | \(C_p\) | 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| Heat‑removal coefficient | \(U A\) | 1500 W K⁻¹ |
| Coolant temperature | \(T_c\) | 298 K |
| Heat of reaction | \(-\Delta H\) | 5.0 × 10⁵ J mol⁻¹ |
| Pre‑exponential factor | \(k_0\) | 1.0 × 10⁶ s⁻¹ |
| Intrinsic activation energy | \(E_a\) | 8.0 × 10⁴ J mol⁻¹ |
| Mass‑transfer coefficient | \(k_{L}a\) | 0.20 s⁻¹ |
| Distribution coefficient | \(K\) | (i) \(10^{-4}\) (ii) \(10^{-2}\) |
| Concentration of B in non‑reacting phase | \(C_B\) | 2.0 mol m⁻³ |
| Initial temperature | \(T(0)\) | 298 K |
| Initial concentration of A | \(C_A(0)\) | 0 mol m⁻³ |

**Task**

4. **Instantaneous reaction limit**
In the limiting case where the reaction is *instantaneous* (i.e., the chemical step is infinitely fast, so \(r_{\text{eff}} = J\) at all times), show analytically that no thermal runaway can occur regardless of the feed rate. Provide a concise proof based on the energy balance and the fact that the reaction heat release is directly proportional to the mass‑transfer flux.
unverified_model_answer:
In the instantaneous‑reaction limit the chemical step is infinitely fast, so the effective rate is always the mass‑transfer flux  

\[
r_{\rm eff}=J=k_{L}a\bigl(C_A^{*}-C_A\bigr)\qquad\bigl({\rm mol\;m^{-3}s^{-1}}\bigr).
\]

---

### 1.  Mass balance in the fast‑reaction limit  

The mole balance for A in the reacting phase is  

\[
\frac{d}{dt}(VC_A)=F-JV .
\]

Because the reaction consumes A as soon as it arrives, the concentration in the reacting phase remains essentially zero \((C_A\approx0)\).  Hence \(d(VC_A)/dt\approx0\) and  

\[
F=JV\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;J=\frac{F}{V}. \tag{1}
\]

Thus the mass‑transfer flux cannot exceed the feed rate; the heat‑release rate is bounded by the feed.

---

### 2.  Energy balance with \(r_{\rm eff}=J\)

Insert (1) into the energy balance  

\[
\rho C_{p}V\frac{dT}{dt}= -UA\,(T-T_c)+(-\Delta H)\,VJ
\]

to obtain  

\[
\rho C_{p}V\frac{dT}{dt}= -UA\,(T-T_c)+(-\Delta H)\,F . \tag{2}
\]

The heat‑generation term \((-\,\Delta H)F\) is **constant** (independent of \(V\) or \(T\)).  Equation (2) can be written as  

\[
\frac{dT}{dt}= -\frac{UA}{\rho C_{p}V}\,(T-T_c)+\frac{(-\Delta H)F}{\rho C_{p}V}. \tag{3}
\]

---

### 3.  Existence of a finite steady state  

Setting \(dT/dt=0\) in (2) gives the unique steady‑state temperature  

\[
T_{\rm ss}=T_c+\frac{(-\Delta H)F}{UA}. \tag{4}
\]

Because \(UA>0\) and \((-\,\Delta H)F\) is finite for any finite feed rate, \(T_{\rm ss}\) is finite.

---

### 4.  No thermal runaway  

From (3) the right–hand side is a linear function of \(T\) with a **negative** coefficient for \(T\).  Consequently  

\[
\frac{dT}{dt}<0\qquad\text{whenever}\qquad T>T_{\rm ss},
\]

so the temperature cannot exceed the bound (4).  Even if the feed rate is increased arbitrarily, the bound simply scales linearly with \(F\) and remains finite; the cooling term \(-UA\,(T-T_c)\) grows without bound with \(T\) and always overcomes the constant heat source.

Hence, in the instantaneous‑reaction (mass‑transfer‑limited) regime the reactor temperature is guaranteed to remain bounded and approach the finite steady state (4); **thermal runaway is impossible for any finite feed rate**.

\[
\boxed{ \displaystyle T(t)\le T_c+\frac{(-\Delta H)F}{UA}\quad\text{for all }t,\;\text{so no thermal runaway can occur.} }
\]

The polymer chains are locally stretched in the vicinity of each multiplet over a distance comparable to the polymer persistence length \(l_{p}\).

In addition, the end‑capping can be achieved either by (i) ion‑exchange of the polymer’s metal counter‑ion with the mesogenic cation, or (ii) proton transfer from a polymer‑bound acidic group (p\(K_{a}^{	ext{acid}}\)) to a tertiary amine moiety on the mesogen (p\(K_{a}^{	ext{amine}}\)).

\[
\begin{aligned}

& q^{*}= \frac{2\pi}{d}\,,\\[4pt]

\]

In the present material each repeat unit consists of an ionic multiplet and the polymer chain that bridges to the next multiplet.  The average distance between two neighboring multiplet centres is therefore set by the polymer’s root‑mean‑square end‑to‑end distance

\[
R_{e}= \sqrt{\langle R^{2}\rangle}= \sqrt{C_{\infty}N}\;l .
\]

Assuming the polymer chain is on average stretched to its RMS size between adjacent aggregates, the inter‑aggregate spacing equals this distance:

\[
d \;\approx\; R_{e}= \sqrt{C_{\infty}N}\;l .
\]

Thus, using the Bragg relation,

\[
q^{*}= \frac{2\pi}{d}= \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{C_{\infty}N}\,l}\, .
\]

\[
\boxed{d = \sqrt{C_{\infty}N}\,l = R_{e}} 
\]

\[
V_{\text{cell}}(\text{cm}^3)=V_{\text{cell}}(\text{Å}^3)\times10^{-24}.

{6.02214076\times10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\times2.5474\times10^{-21}\ \text{cm}^3}\\[2pt]

&=1.101\ \text{g cm}^{-3}=1.101\ \text{Mg m}^{-3}.

where the constants satisfy \(\alpha_b<0,\;\beta_b>0,\;\alpha_x>0,\;\beta_x<0\). Assume that at the reference state \((S=0,\;x=0)\) the cloud point is \(T_c(0,0)=T_0\).
